![](data:image/png;base64,)Precipitated droplets _in-situ_ cross-linking polymerization towards hydrogel beads for ultrahigh removal of positively charged toxins

Jiarui Yin[a](#_bookmark0), Wei Sun[b](#_bookmark1), Xin Song[a](#_bookmark0), Haifeng Ji[a](#_bookmark0), Ye Yang[a](#_bookmark0), Shudong Sun[a](#_bookmark0), Weifeng Zhao[a](#_bookmark0),[c](#_bookmark2),[⁎](#_bookmark4),

a _College of Polymer Science and Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Polymer Materials Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu 610065, China_

b _Laboratory Department of General Hospital of Western Theatek Command, Chengdu 610000, China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

One-pot

Hydrogel particles

_In-situ_ cross-linking polymerization Ultrahigh removal

Positively charged toxins

A B S T R A C T

Green, simple and fast approach towards functional spherical hydrogels with excellent adsorption capacity of toxins remains a huge challenge. Herein, we developed a novel approach to fabricate functional spherical hy-drogel absorbent in 40 s without any post-treatments, for which only water and corn oil were used as green solvents. Acrylic acid (AA) and 2-acrylamido-2-methyl-propanesulfonic acid (AMPS) were selected as functional monomers to produce P(AA-_co_\-AMPS) hydrogel spheres via precipitated droplets _in-situ_ cross-linking poly-merization. Various mass ratios of monomers for the preparation of functional spherical hydrogels were tested to obtain the maximum removal of positively charged toxins. As a result, the adsorption amounts of methylene blue (MB) and Pb2+ could reach as high as 4463.3 and 6393.4 mg/g, respectively. In addition, the particles showed a stable adsorption capacity for at least three desorption-resorption cycles. Therefore, we prepared promising absorbents for ultrahigh removal of positively charged toxins via chemical cross-linking during processing, and the proposed green, one-pot and fast approach has great potential for industrial production of functional spherical hydrogels.

1. Introduction

The elimination of hazardous pollutants from wastewater is a key of holding environmental balance [\[1–4\]](#_bookmark17). Since large amounts of waste-water comes from industries such as textile [\[5\]](#_bookmark18), paper [\[6\]](#_bookmark19), printing [\[7\]](#_bookmark20), mining [\[8\]](#_bookmark21), food technology [\[9\]](#_bookmark22), petrochemical [\[10\]](#_bookmark23), agricultural craft

[\[11\]](#_bookmark24) and son on, there are various pollutants in untreated wastewater, including organic dyes, heavy metal ions, additional agents, con-taminated oil, pesticides, fertilizers and other inorganic/organic pol-lutants. Charged surface is a common feature for most pollutants. Among these pollutants, cationic dyes are classified as positively charged toxins. For instance, methylene blue (MB) as a typical cationic dye could cause high blood pressure, mental disorder, nausea, and abdominal pain, etc.[\[12\]](#_bookmark25).Therefore, it is urgent to eliminate positively charged toxins before discharging. Adsorption is considered as the most effective method, owning to its low cost, simplicity of design and op-eration, lack of harmful by-products [\[13\]](#_bookmark26).

In recent years, various methods for preparing absorbents have been

developed for the removal of positively charged toxins. For instance, emulsion polymerization [\[14,15\]](#_bookmark27), suspension polymerization [\[16–18\]](#_bookmark28), precipitation polymerization [\[19\]](#_bookmark29) and the modification on the matrixes (activated carbon [\[20\]](#_bookmark30), chitosan [\[21,22\]](#_bookmark31), cellulose [\[23–25\]](#_bookmark32) and sodium alginate [\[26\]](#_bookmark33)). However, many kinds of hazardous organic solvents and additional agents are employed during the preparation process, and the purification of the absorbents is energy-consuming and inevitable. In addition, the purification process also generates wastewater [\[27\]](#_bookmark34), which seems to be an intractable contradiction. Besides, the production processes are also relatively complicated [\[28–30\]](#_bookmark35) and time-consuming [\[31,32\]](#_bookmark37), it is ordinary for these approaches to suffer from several pre-paration steps. Therefore, a green and simple approach towards ad-sorbents is desired.

Increasing the adsorption amount is of paramount importance for

adsorption, besides making the preparation green, and simplifying the processes of reaction and molding. To increase the adsorption amounts of cation dyes, such as methylene blue (MB), many studies focused on increasing the functional groups in the adsorbents [\[33,34\]](#_bookmark38). As an

example, with few functional groups, polydopamine microspheres could adsorb 90.7 mg/g for MB [\[35\]](#_bookmark39). While introducing graphene oxide which possessed more functional groups into substrate, graphene oxide/chitosan aerogel microspheres removed 584.6 mg/g for MB [\[36\]](#_bookmark40). Thakur et al. introduced functional monomer AA into the adsorbent, and SA-cl-poly(AA)-TiO2 hydrogel nanocomposite showed a maximum adsorption amount of 2257.4 mg/g for MB [\[37\]](#_bookmark41). Recently, we prepared P(AMPS-co-AA) hydrogel particles for the adsorption of MB (2967 mg/ g)[\[38\]](#_bookmark42). However, the adsorption capacity is not ideal because of the following items: (1) the monomers in reaction solution could not be completely soaked into the capsule; (2) partial functional monomers would be leached out through the porous shell during subsequent thermal reaction. Above all, the increase in the compositions of func-tional groups are beneficial in the adsorption of positively charged toxins by increasing the ion exchange capacity [\[39,40\]](#_bookmark43).

Herein, we aimed to propose an advanced green and simple ap-

proach towards functional spherical hydrogel particles with ultrahigh adsorption amount for positively charged toxins. AA and AMPS were used to fabricate P(AA-co-AMPS) hydrogel particles via precipitated droplets _in-situ_ cross-linking polymerization. Briefly, homogeneous re-action aqueous solution (monomers, initiator, cross-linker and water) was prepared firstly. Then, the aqueous solution was dripped in the hot corn oil successively. Aqueous droplets settled in the hot corn oil which was heated by external 90 °C circulating water. The polymerization for spherical hydrogel particles was completed during the short time of sedimentation. The structural characterizations of the hydrogel parti-cles were performed by using Fourier transform infrared spectrum (FTIR), thermo gravimetric analysis (TGA), scanning electron micro-scopy (SEM) and ion exchange capacity (IEC) methods. The application of P(AA-co-AMPS) as absorbent for the removals of MB and heavy metal ions was also investigated. Furthermore, the influence of various con-ditions such as contact time, dye concentration and pH on the ad-sorption behaviors were studied, and the adsorption kinetics and iso-therms were calculated to understand the eﬃciency of the adsorbent.

1. Experimental section
    1. _Materials_

Acrylic acid (AA, AR, > 99%), 2-acrylamide-2-methylpropane-sulfonic acid (AMPS, 98%), ammonium persulfate (APS, AR, ≥98%), _N_,_N_'-methylenebis (acrylamide) (MBA, for molecular biology,

≥99.0%), sodium hydroxide (NaOH, ACS, 97%), methylene blue (MB, 99%), methyl orange (MO, 96%), AgNO3, CuSO4, Pb(NO3)2, CrCl3 and FeCl3 were received from Aladdin. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) was ob-tained from Chengdu Kelong Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd., and used as received. The corn oil was purchased from general supermarket, and deionized (DI) water was home-made.

- 1.  _Fabrication and characterizations of hydrogel particles_

The hydrogel particles were fabricated using precipitated droplets _in-situ_ cross-linking polymerization. In brief, the given amounts of monomer, initiator APS and cross-linker MBA were dissolved in DI water, then ultrasonically oscillated for 5 min at room temperature. Subsequently, the precursor aqueous solution was added into a 10-mL syringe, through the injection needle (0.5 mm diameter), the uniform and spherical droplets were obtained and then successively dripped into the sedimentation column filled with hot corn oil. The reaction tem-perature was maintained at 90 °C with hot circulating water outside. The droplets were slowly settled to the bottom of the corn oil because of the density and insolubility. Typically, it took about 40 s to complete the sedimentation in which the polymerization of spherical hydrogel particles was completed. Finally, the hydrogel spheres were sedimented from the oil phase to the DI water for collection, since the stirring broke the tension at the oil-water interface (as shown in [Scheme 1](#_bookmark5)).

The total monomer amount was 20 wt% of the whole solution system, and the mass ratios of the AA to AMPS were 5:0, 4:1, 3:2, 2:3, 1:4 and 0:5, respectively. 4 wt% APS and 10 wt% MBA to the monomers were used to prepare hydrogel particles, and they were named as P x-y, “x-y” meant the mass ratio of AA and AMPS in the solution. For example, “P 4-1” represented that the mass ratio of AA and AMPS was 4:1.

The water uptake ratios of the hydrogel particles were tested by a typical gravimetric method. 50 hydrogel particles were dried under vacuum at 70 °C for 24 h to reach constant dry weights. Then, the particles were immersed in DI water for 24 h to swell completely again, the weights of swelling particles were measured. During this process, the diameters of the spherical hydrogel particles were also measured. Finally, the mass swelling ratio (_Rm_) and volume swelling ratio (_Rv_) were obtained from the followed equations:

Attenuated total reflection Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR, Nicolet 560, USA) was used to characterize the chemical structures of PAA, P 4-1, P 3-2, P 2-3, P 1-4 and PAMPS. Data were recorded between 4000 and 400 cm−1 at a resolution of 2 cm−1, and FTIR spectra were obtained according to the data between 2000 and 800 cm−1 for better observation.

Thermogravimetric analyzer (METTLLE TOLEDO, TGA/DSC 3+, Switzerland) was employed to characterize the components of the freeze-dried samples, the TGA data was obtained under a dry N2 at-mosphere from 30 °C to 800 °C at a heating speed of 10 °C/min, and the derivative thermogravimetric analysis (DTG) curves were also received from TGA.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Phenom Pure, Phenom World, Netherlands) was employed to characterize the surface and cross-sec-tion morphologies of the hydrogel particles.

- 1.  _Ion exchange capacity (IEC)_

As the hydrogel particles are used as adsorbent based on electro-static interaction, the tests for their ion exchange capacities (IEC) are necessary. Acid–base titration is the most appealing method for the determination of IEC because of its directness and simplicity [\[41\]](#_bookmark44). Several hydrogel particles were first incubated with 0.01 mol/L NaOH and 0.01 mol/L HCl solution in turns for 3 cycles, during the process, DI water was employed in between to remove residual solution on the surface of the hydrogel particles. Afterward, the hydrogel particles were incubated in 0.01 mol/L NaOH and 0.01 mol/L HCl solution for extra 24 h, the volumes of the solutions were about twice the volume of the theoretical IEC from calculation, which assumed that all the carboxyl and sulfonic acid groups could be completely protonated. Finally, the HCl solution was titrated with standard NaOH solution (0.01 mol/L). The experimental IEC was calculated by the following formula:

- 1.  _Desorption-resorption test_

To study the recyclability, several hydrogel particles with optimal adsorption performance were put into 20 mL of 1000 μmol/L MB so-lution at pH 7 at room temperature until reaching equilibrium. Then, the hydrogel particles were taken out, washed with DI water and im-mersed into 50 mL of 1 mol/L HCl solution for desorption until reaching

equilibrium. During the process, the HCl solution was changed at in-tervals and the absorbance of the solution was then measured. Five cycles of desorption–resorption process was repeated.

ATR-FTIR spectroscopy was used to characterize the chemical structure of the hydrogel particles ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark10)(a) and (d)). The strong ab-sorption peak observed at 1710 cm−1 was attributed to the C\]O stretching vibration of carboxyl groups from the monomer AA. The strong absorption peak observed at 1037 cm−1 was corresponding to S\]O stretching vibration of the sulfonic acid group from the monomer AMPS. In addition, the adsorption peaks at 1634 cm−1, 1540 cm−1, 1446 cm−1 and 1390 cm−1 were corresponding to the C\]O stretching vibration, the NeH bending vibration and the CeN stretching vibration of secondary amide group in cross-linker MBA and monomer AMPS. The appearance or high intensity of the characteristic adsorption peaks mentioned above confirmed the successful synthesis of prospective products.

In order to investigate the thermal stabilities and compositions of

the various hydrogel particles, thermo gravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed. As illustrated in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark10)(b) and (c), the pure PAA exhibited three stages for mass loss. The first stage accompanied with ca. 12% loss in the interval of 70–180 °C was due to the loss of water [\[42\]](#_bookmark45). The second stage accompanied with ca. 37% loss in the range of 190–330 °C with a maximum decomposition rate at 270 °C (_Tm1_) was attributed to the dehydration and decarboxylation of eCOOH in PAA [\[43\]](#_bookmark46). The third

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

stage accompanied with ca. 42% loss in the range of 335–540 °C with a maximum decomposition rate at 390 °C (_Tm2_) was because of the de-gradation of the polymer backbone. While the pure PAMPS exhibited four stages for mass loss. The first stage accompanied with ca. 17% loss in the interval of 40–170 °C was attributed to the loss of water. The second stage accompanied with ca. 7% loss in the range of 170–210 °C with a maximum decomposition rate at 195 °C (_Tm3_) was attributed to the dehydration of eSO3H in PAMPS. The third stage accompanied with ca. 49% loss in the range of 210–330 °C with a maximum decomposi-tion rate at 310 °C (_Tm4_) was attributed to the desulfonation of eSO3H in PAMPS. The fourth stage accompanied with ca. 17% loss in the range of 335–515 °C with a maximum decomposition rate at 415 °C (_Tm5_) was attributed to the degradation of the polymer backbone.

However, for the copolymers P 4-1, P 3-2, P 2-3 and P 1-4, besides

the stage for the loss of water, there were only two main stages for mass loss. The mass loss in the range of 190–330 °C was corresponding to the degradation of eCOOH and eSO3H, in which the two degradation peaks of eCOOH and eSO3H overlapped and formed a wider peak, from [Fig. 2](#_bookmark10)(c) and (f). With increasing the mass ratio of AMPS, the range of stage expanded, and the temperature accompanied with maximum decomposition rate also increased (250, 270, 275 and 306 °C for P 4-1, P 3-2, P 2-3 and P 1-4, respectively). The other stage was attributed to degradation of the copolymer backbone. Therefore, all the hydrogel particles were thermal stable below 190 °C.

The morphologies of the hydrogel particles were characterized by SEM. As illustrated in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark11), for the hydrogel particles containing AA, there were many small uniform pores but nearly no obvious cracks on the surface. From left to right, the distribution of the pores became less uniform, with increasing the mass ratio of AMPS. While for the pure PAMPS hydrogel particle, there were obvious long cracks rather than small pores on the relatively smoother surface. Similarly, on the cross section views of the hydrogel particles, typical pores for PAA gradually changed into irregular folds, and collapsed sheets, with increasing the mass ratio of monomer AMPS. Briefly, the cross section views of the hydrogels became rougher. Furthermore, the cross section view of pure PAMPS hydrogel particle appeared different, there were several large

cavities in the center. The results demonstrated that copolymer hy-drogel particles had both rough surface and porous cross section, which would benefit high removal of the dyes and heavy metal ions.

- 1.  _Ion exchange capacity (IEC)_

IEC is an important indicator for adsorbents based on electrostatic attraction, which means the theoretical amount of charged adsorbate that the adsorbent can neutralize. The experimental IEC values and theoretical IEC values are shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark12)(a). The IECexp for PAA, P 4-1, P 3-2, P 2-3, P 1-4 and PAMPS were 12.41, 10.19, 8.19, 6.34, 5.53 and

3.22 mequiv/g, respectively. The decrease of IECexp matched the de-crease of molar amounts of functional monomers. It was also illustrated that IECexp was lower than the IECtheo, since the adsorption sites of the hydrogel particles could not be fully occupied. Furthermore, the IECexp were higher than 3 mequiv/g since they were made by cross-linking of charged monomers without any other substrates, which were the highest level of IEC among all the ion-exchange materials at present [\[29,44–46\]](#_bookmark36).

- 1.  _Adsorption experiments_
        1. _The selective adsorption capacity_

The hydrogel particles were all supposed to show much better ad-sorption capacity to positively charged toxins than negatively charged toxins owing to the electrostatic interaction. Here, MB (cationic dye) and MO (anionic dye) were chosen as the models for the selective ad-sorption.

As illustrated in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark12)(c) and (d), the hydrogel particles showed a better adsorption capacity to MB than MO, according to the adsorption amounts and obvious color changes. Compared with the control sample MB, the color of MB solutions with 3 hydrogel particles became lighter after adsorption, the adsorption amounts of each sample were 610.61, 712.38, 695.81, 667.86, 613.11 and 523.08 mg/g, respectively, and their removal ratios were all higher than 97%. It meant all hydrogel particles exhibited a good adsorption capacity to MB dye. As for MO,

shown in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark12)(b). Three typical kinetic models (pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order and the intraparticle diffusion equation) were used to detect the adsorption process towards MB. The pseudo-first-order model assumes that the adsorption of adsorbate from the solution to the surface of the adsorbent is controlled by the diffusion step. The pseudo-second-order model assumes that the adsorption process is controlled by the chemical adsorption mechanism, the equations for calculation of the adsorption amount at equilibrium (_qe_) and correlation coeﬃcients (_r2_) for the adsorption process of various samples towards

MB at the initial concentration of 1000 μmol/L were provided in sup-

porting information, and the data were listed in [Table 3](#_bookmark13).

For pseudo-first-order model, the _r2_ values of these samples were lower than 0.94, only the _r2_ value of P 1-4 was a little higher than 0.97, furthermore, the theoretical _qe_ calculated from the model were far away from the experimental _qe_. For pseudo-second-order model, the _r2_ values were all high than 0.99, which meant the strict linear relationship be-tween _t/qt_ and _t_. Furthermore, the theoretical _qe_ calculated from the model were next to the experimental _qe_. It could be found that the pseudo-second-order model fitted very well with the adsorption process

towards MB for PAA, P 4-1, P 3-2, P 2-3, P 1-4 and PAMPS. Thus, the adsorption rates of the functional hydrogel particles were controlled by the chemical adsorption.

We also used the intraparticle diffusion model to analyze the data (Fig. S1), and the detailed information was provided in supporting in-formation.

The adsorption process for each sample could be divided into three step stages. In general, the time ranges of three step stages were not the same for various samples. For each sample, _kp_I > _kp_II > _kp_III, and _kp_III was much lower than _kp_I and _kp_II, which meant the first stage and the second stage played important roles in the whole adsorption process. The _r 2_ and _r 2_ values were almost higher than 0.96, while _r 2_ values are mostly not very appropriate due that (1) the adsorption ratios at this time were already very low or even drop to 0; (2) some measurement errors ( ± 20 mg/g for the last 3 _qt_ for P 2-3, ± 5 mg/g for the last 3 _qt_

- -   1.  _Adsorption isotherms_

The adsorption isotherms were also studied in detail, since it could provide information about the saturated adsorption capacity for ad-sorbents under certain conditions. Here, the adsorption amounts of MB for the hydrogel particles at different initial concentrations were stu-died, as shown in Fig. S2(a), P 1-4 and PAMPS were listed in Fig. S2(d), since the growth of their adsorption amounts had not reached a satu-

rated stage at an initial concentration of 1000 μmol/L. Two typical

isotherm models (Langmuir isotherm and Freundlich isotherm) were used to analyze the MB adsorption behaviors, and the equations for expression of two models were provided in supporting information.

As illustrated in Fig. S2(b), (e) and [Table 4](#_bookmark14), there was an obviously strict linear relationship between _Ce/qe_ and _Ce_, and the _r 2_ values were all higher than 0.98, which meant the Langmuir isotherm model was suitable for the adsorption process, and the adsorption towards MB was monolayer chemical adsorption on uniform surface. Furthermore, the _qmax_ of PAA, P 4-1, P 3-2 and P 2-3 calculated from the equation were very close to their experimental _qe_ at an initial concentration of

_L_

1000 μmol/L, which meant the external and internal surfaces of these

hydrogel particles had been covered with a single layer of MB mole-cules at this time. It was worth emphasized that the _qmax_ of P 1-4 and PAMPS calculated from the equation were 4447.03 and 4439.00 mg/g, respectively, meanwhile, the experimental _qe_ of P 1-4 were always higher than those of PAMPS at the same initial concentration, thus P 1-4 preformed best in these hydrogel particles for the adsorption of MB.

However, for the Freundlich model, as shown in Fig. S2(c) and (f), the fitting lines obviously deviated a lot from the data points, and the _r 2_ values (0.96562, 0.88804, 0.75622, 0.65099, 0.91383 and 0.92433)

_F_

were almost very low, all lower than the _rL2_ values, which indicated the Freundlich model did not fit the MB adsorption process.

The remarkable adsorption capacity of P 1-4 hydrogel particles was because that: (1) P 1-4 was made by cross-linking of charged monomers without any substrates; (2) P 1-4 possessed a porous structure according to the SEM images ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark11)); (3) it possessed a high IECexp value ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark12)a).

- -   1.  _Adsorption of P 1-4 hydrogel particles for heavy metal ions_

The capability of removing heavy metal ions from the polluted water was also important because of the contamination of water and soil environment [\[48\]](#_bookmark48). 3 hydrogel particles with the optimal adsorption capacity were immersed into respective AgNO3, CuSO4, Pb(NO3)2, CrCl3 and FeCl3 aqueous solutions (20 mL, 40 mmol/L) at room tem-perature with continuous oscillation. After 3 days, the saturated ad-sorption amounts of P 1-4 for Ag+, Cu2+, Pb2+, Fe3+ and Cr3+ were 491.80, 327.87, 6393.44, 3524.59 and 262.30 mg/g, respectively. The different adsorption amounts for different heavy metal ions may be owing to the combination of numerous influence factors, including hydration diameters, hydration enthalpies, ionic potential, electro-negativity and relative atomic mass [\[49\]](#_bookmark49). As shown in Table S4, the Pb2+ showed smaller hydration radii, lower hydration enthalpy, higher ionic potential, higher electronegativity and higher relative atomic mass, which results in its highest adsorption amount. Remarkably, in this study, P 1-4 showed an ultrahigh adsorption capacity for Pb2+, compared with other adsorbents. For instance, sodium acrylate and acrylamide copolymer/GO hydrogels showed a maximum adsorption amount of 452.3 mg/g for Pb2+ [\[50\]](#_bookmark50). Poly(acrylic acid) grafted chit-osan hydrogel exhibited an adsorption amount of 734.3 mg/g for Pb2+ [\[51\]](#_bookmark51). Anionic surfactant-templated amino-functionalized mesoporous silica showed a maximum adsorption amount of 982.1 mg/g for Pb2+ [\[52\]](#_bookmark52). Poly-amidoamine dendrimer/carbon nanotubes nanocomposite showed a maximum adsorption amount of 4870 mg/g for Pb2+ [\[53\]](#_bookmark53).

For the investigation of the adsorption appearance of P 1-4 in

complex conditions, we prepared a mixture solution consist of Pb (NO3)2 and MB, while their concentrations were 20 mmol/L and 1000 μmol/L, respectively, and the pictures of the mixture solution before and after adsorption are shown in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark15)(b). The P 1-4 hydrogel particles after adsorption were gray and smaller, while they were navy

blue and bigger in pure MB solution. Besides, the adsorption amounts for Pb2+ and MB were 4590.16 and 1175.83 mg/g, respectively. P 1-4 trended to absorb more Pb2+ than MB, because of the smaller mole-cular diameter of Pb2+ (the diameter of Pb2+ is approximately 120 pm while that of MB is approximately 0.9 nm [\[54\]](#_bookmark54)). Above all, P 1-4 showed high adsorption capacity to positively charged toxins in com-plex conditions.

- 1.  _Acid and alkali resistances of the hydrogel particles_

Since both AA and AMPS have negatively charged groups, the hy-drogel particles show a characteristic: shrinking in the acidic environ-ment and swelling in the alkaline environment. As expected, the dia-meter of the hydrogel particles gradually increased in order of pH from low to high, after soaking in the solutions with different pH for 7 days. The hydrogel particles were further dyed by MB for clearer observation (the colors of solutions changed at pH = 0, 13 and 14 because that MB

The pH value of the solution not only affects the particle size of the hydrogel particles, but also affects the adsorption capacity of the hy-drogel particles towards MB. Three P 1-4 hydrogel particles were put into 1 mol/L HCl solution, neutral DI water, and 1 mol/L NaOH solution for 24 h, then taken out and put into 20 mL 2000 μmol/L MB aqueous

solutions for saturated adsorption, the adsorption amounts were

2780.79, 4319.18 and 4807.41 mg/g, respectively, there was a sig-nificant reduction in adsorption capacity after soaking in HCl solution while remarkable increase in NaOH solution, compared with soaking in neutral DI water, as shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark16)(b). The adsorption capacity after soaking in HCl solution remained 64.38% of the original value, while the adsorption capacity after soaking in NaOH solution increased to 111.30% of the original value, which could also confirm that the ad-sorption capacity of the hydrogel particles for MB dye was owing to the electrostatic interaction between the charged functional groups and MB.

- 1.  _Desorption-resorption test_

Recyclability is a crucial limitation for many adsorbents applying in removing toxins from polluted water. In order to determine the re-cyclability of hydrogel particles, the desorption-resorption test of the P 1-4 was carried out. HCl solution was employed as de-sorbent by ad-justing the surface charge of hydrogel particles because the adsorption of MB was based on the electrostatic interaction. From [Fig. 6](#_bookmark16)(c), it was realized that the HCl solution was replaced 5 times during the complete desorption process owing to the high adsorption capacity (2890.0 mg/ g) of the P 1-4 hydrogel particles. Meanwhile, as shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark16)(d), the

first desorption ratio reached up to 88.10% and the first resorption ratio was 87.55% of the origin adsorption capacity, even after 5 desorption-resorption cycles, the hydrogel particles still maintained 79.63% of the origin adsorption capacity, which meant the P 1-4 hydrogel particles had long-term reuse capability for adsorption.

1. Conclusions

In this study, we successfully synthesized several kinds of functional spherical hydrogel particles via a completely green, simple and fast approach. In 40 s, the hydrogel particles with uniform particle size could be produced in large-scale. This high eﬃciency method has po-tential applications for producing more types of hydrogel particles. P 1-4 preformed the best adsorption ability for positively charged toxins since it exhibited ultrahigh adsorption capacity and relatively high adsorption rate for positively charged toxins. Meanwhile, P 1-4 pos-sessed porous structure, the highest level of IEC, good thermal stability and recyclability. The MB adsorption kinetic fitted the pseudo-first-order model and the intraparticle diffusion model well, meanwhile, the adsorption isotherm fitted the Langmuir model well. The saturated adsorption amount towards MB was as high as 4463.3 mg/g by calcu-lated from the Langmuir model, which was close to the experimental adsorption amount. It was noticed that the pH showed great influence on the amount of adsorption, and desorption could be achieved by adjusting the system to acidic, and the P 1-4 could be recycled by im-mersed in HCl solution. With the advantages of easy preparation, ul-trahigh adsorption capacity, high adsorption rate, good recyclability, P 1-4 is believed to be used as effective adsorbent to remove positively charged toxins from wastewater.

5 Novelty statement

We developed a novel approach to fabricate functional spherical hydrogel absorbents in 40 s without any post-treatments, for which

only water and corn oil were used as green solvents. The prepared P (AA-_co_\-AMPS) hydrogel spheres showed advantages of easy producing, uniform particle size, ultrahigh removal capacity towards positively charged toxins with good reusability, which are promising to be ef-fective absorbents in wastewater treatment.
